turns.label: q1
turns.question:
Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO4 • 5 H2O, is a blue crystalline solid. Upon gentle heating, it loses water to form anhydrous CuSO4, which is a white solid.
a. When 5.000 g CuSO4 • 5H2O is heated to remove all of its water, what mass of anhydrous CuSO4 will be produced?
b. Explain the change in color on dehydration of CuSO4 • 5 H2O.
c. A solution of 0.0506 g Cu(CH3COO)2 • H2O is made up with water to a volume of 5.00 mL water. This solution in a 1-cm cuvette produces a visible spectrum with a maximum absorption at 763 nm. What wavelength would be the best choice to determine the concentration of Cu(II)?
d. A student determines the value of n in an unknown crystalline hydrate of copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NO3)2 • n H2O, by preparing 5.00 mL of an aqueous solution of a known mass of the compound and measuring its absorbance at the wavelength determined in part c. However, the student inserts the cuvette into the spectrophotometer without first wiping fingerprints from it. How will this affect the value of n determined in the experiment?
e. An alternative method for determining the degree of hydration of the copper nitrate is to allow a known mass of compound to react with excess KI solution, which produces a yellow-brown suspension. Write a balanced net ionic equation for this reaction.
f. The experiment in part e is carried out with 0.1000 g of the hydrated copper(II) nitrate. To the resulting mixture is added a 0.0250 M solution of sodium thiosulfate, Na2S2O3, until the color of the mixture has just dissipated, leaving a milky white suspension. This requires 17.20 mL of added sodium thiosulfate solution. What is the value of n for the Cu(NO3)2 • n H2O?
turns.official_answer:
a. 3.196 g
b. Dehydration changes the ligand environment around Cu(II) from water to sulfate; the d-d absorption shifts out of the visible/into the near-IR, so the solid appears white.
c. 763 nm
d. It will give a smaller value of n.
e. 2 Cu2+(aq) + 5 I-(aq) -> 2 CuI(s) + I3-(aq)
f. n = 2.50

[DERIVED RUBRIC]
Part a: 2 points (1 pt for moles of hydrate, 1 pt for mass of anhydrous).
Part b: 2 points (1 pt for mentioning d9/ligand field change, 1 pt for shift of absorption to near-IR).
Part c: 2 points (2 pts for 763 nm).
Part d: 2 points (1 pt for increased apparent absorbance, 1 pt for concluding smaller n).
Part e: 2 points (2 pts for correct balanced net ionic equation).
Part f: 2 points (1 pt for moles of Cu2+, 1 pt for correct calculation of n).
Total: 12 points.
turns.candidate_answer:
a. Molar masses (using Cu = 63.55, S = 32.07, O = 16.00, H = 1.008):

\[
M(\text{CuSO}_4)=63.55+32.07+4(16.00)=159.62\ \text{g/mol}
\]

\[
M(5\text{H}_2\text{O})=5(18.016)=90.08\ \text{g/mol}
\]

\[
M(\text{CuSO}_4\cdot 5\text{H}_2\text{O})=249.70\ \text{g/mol}
\]

The fraction of the hydrate that becomes anhydrous CuSO₄ is

\[
\frac{159.62}{249.70}=0.63925
\]

So from 5.000 g hydrate:

\[
5.000\text{ g}\times 0.63925=3.196\text{ g}
\]

\[
\boxed{3.196\text{ g CuSO}_4}
\]

---

b. In hydrated copper(II) sulfate, water molecules act as ligands coordinated to the Cu²⁺ ion. These ligands split the copper(II) \(d\)-orbitals in a way that causes absorption of visible light, giving the compound its blue color.

When the compound is dehydrated, the ligand environment around Cu²⁺ changes because coordinated water molecules are removed. This changes the \(d\)-orbital splitting and therefore changes the wavelengths of light absorbed. Anhydrous CuSO₄ does not absorb visible light strongly in the same way, so it appears white.

\[
\boxed{\text{The color change is due to a change in the ligand field around Cu}^{2+}\text{ when water is removed.}}
\]

---

c. The best wavelength for determining the concentration of Cu(II) is the wavelength of maximum absorbance, because it gives greatest sensitivity.

The maximum absorption is at 763 nm.

\[
\boxed{763\text{ nm}}
\]

---

d. Fingerprints on the cuvette would absorb and/or scatter additional light. This would make the measured absorbance appear too high.

By Beer’s law,

\[
A=\varepsilon bc
\]

a higher absorbance would be interpreted as a higher Cu²⁺ concentration. For a fixed mass of the hydrate sample, this means the student would conclude that the sample contains more copper(II) nitrate formula units and therefore less water per formula unit.

Thus the calculated value of \(n\) would be too low.

\[
\boxed{\text{The measured }n\text{ would be too low.}}
\]

---

e. Copper(II) oxidizes iodide to iodine, while copper(II) is reduced to copper(I), which precipitates as CuI. The yellow-brown color comes from iodine/triiodide in solution.

Balanced net ionic equation:

\[
\boxed{2\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+4\text{I}^-(aq)\rightarrow 2\text{CuI}(s)+\text{I}_2(aq)}
\]

Equivalently, since excess iodide is present and iodine forms triiodide:

\[
\boxed{2\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)+5\text{I}^-(aq)\rightarrow 2\text{CuI}(s)+\text{I}_3^-(aq)}
\]

---

f. The iodine produced is titrated with thiosulfate:

\[
\text{I}_2+2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}\rightarrow 2\text{I}^-+\text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}
\]

Moles of thiosulfate used:

\[
0.0250\ \text{mol/L}\times 0.01720\ \text{L}=4.300\times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}
\]

Thus moles of iodine:

\[
n(\text{I}_2)=\frac{4.300\times 10^{-4}}{2}=2.150\times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}
\]

From part e:

\[
2\text{Cu}^{2+}\rightarrow \text{I}_2
\]

So moles of Cu²⁺, and therefore moles of copper(II) nitrate hydrate, are

\[
n(\text{Cu}^{2+})=2(2.150\times 10^{-4})=4.300\times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}
\]

The molar mass of the hydrate is therefore

\[
M=\frac{0.1000\ \text{g}}{4.300\times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}}
=232.56\ \text{g/mol}
\]

Molar mass of anhydrous copper(II) nitrate:

\[
M(\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2)=63.55+2(14.01+3(16.00))
\]

\[
=63.55+2(62.01)=187.57\ \text{g/mol}
\]

Mass due to water per mole:

\[
232.56-187.57=44.99\ \text{g/mol}
\]

\[
n=\frac{44.99}{18.016}=2.50
\]

\[
\boxed{n=2.50}
\]

So the formula is approximately

\[
\boxed{\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2\cdot 2.5\text{H}_2\text{O}}
\]

turns.question:
Calcium oxalate, CaC2O4, has a Ksp of 2.7 × 10-9. Oxalic acid, H2C2O4, has two ionizable hydrogens with pKa1 = 1.27 and pKa2 = 4.28.
a. Draw a Lewis structure for oxalate ion, C2O42-, including all bonds, lone pairs, and formal charges.
b. Calculate the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in pure water.
c. Calculate the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in a 0.100 M CaCl2 solution.
d. A 0.100 mol sample of solid CaC2O4 is suspended in 1.00 L of water and HCl(g) is bubbled through the solution until all of the solid just dissolves. What is the pH of the final homogeneous solution? You may assume the final volume of solution is 1.00 L.
e. How many moles of HCl(g) are added in part d?
f. Will the molar solubility of CaC2O4 in 0.1 M NaHC2O4 be significantly greater than, significantly less than, or within 10% of the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in pure water? Justify your answer.
turns.official_answer:
a. [O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O]2- (with resonance structures)
b. 5.2 x 10-5 mol L-1
c. 2.7 x 10-8 mol L-1
d. pH = -0.51
e. 3.4 mol
f. Significantly less than.

Part a: 2 points (2 pts for correct Lewis structure with formal charges).
Part b: 2 points (2 pts for correct solubility).
Part c: 2 points (2 pts for correct solubility).
Part d: 3 points (1 pt for setting up combined Ka expression, 1 pt for [H+], 1 pt for pH).
Part e: 2 points (1 pt for H+ concentration contribution, 1 pt for protonation of oxalate contribution).
Part f: 2 points (1 pt for 'significantly less than', 1 pt for justification using common ion effect and calculation).
Total: 13 points.
turns.candidate_answer:
a. Oxalate ion is

\[
\ce{C2O4^{2-}}
\]

A Lewis structure can be drawn as two carboxylate groups bonded together:

\[
\boxed{\ce{^-O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O^-}}
\]

Each carbon is bonded to the other carbon, one double-bonded oxygen, and one single-bonded oxygen.

- Each double-bonded O has 2 lone pairs and formal charge 0.
- Each single-bonded O has 3 lone pairs and formal charge \(-1\).
- Each carbon has formal charge 0.

There are resonance structures in which the double bond and negative charge are delocalized within each carboxylate group.

---

b. For

\[
\ce{CaC2O4(s) <=> Ca^{2+}(aq) + C2O4^{2-}(aq)}
\]

\[
K_{sp}=[\ce{Ca^{2+}}][\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]=2.7\times 10^{-9}
\]

If calcium oxalate dissolves in pure water with molar solubility \(s\), then initially

\[
[\ce{Ca^{2+}}]=s
\]

The oxalate is a weak base, so not all dissolved oxalate remains as \(\ce{C2O4^{2-}}\). However, because \(\ce{HC2O4^-}\) has

\[
K_a2=10^{-4.28}=5.25\times 10^{-5}
\]

and the solution will be only mildly basic, essentially all dissolved oxalate remains as \(\ce{C2O4^{2-}}\). Thus,

\[
K_{sp}\approx s^2
\]

\[
s=\sqrt{2.7\times 10^{-9}}
\]

\[
s=5.2\times 10^{-5}\ \text{M}
\]

\[
\boxed{5.2\times 10^{-5}\ \text{M}}
\]

---

c. In \(0.100\ \text{M}\ \ce{CaCl2}\),

\[
[\ce{Ca^{2+}}]\approx 0.100\ \text{M}
\]

\[
K_{sp}=[\ce{Ca^{2+}}][\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]
\]

\[
[\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]=\frac{2.7\times 10^{-9}}{0.100}
=2.7\times 10^{-8}\ \text{M}
\]

Thus the molar solubility is approximately

\[
\boxed{2.7\times 10^{-8}\ \text{M}}
\]

---

d. If \(0.100\ \text{mol}\) of \(\ce{CaC2O4}\) dissolves in \(1.00\ \text{L}\), then

\[
[\ce{Ca^{2+}}]=0.100\ \text{M}
\]

At the point where all solid just dissolves, the solution is saturated with respect to \(\ce{CaC2O4}\), so

\[
[\ce{Ca^{2+}}][\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]=K_{sp}
\]

\[
[\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]=\frac{2.7\times 10^{-9}}{0.100}
=2.7\times 10^{-8}\ \text{M}
\]

The total dissolved oxalate concentration is

\[
C_T=0.100\ \text{M}
\]

For oxalic acid,

\[
\ce{H2C2O4 <=> H+ + HC2O4^-}
\]

\[
K_{a1}=10^{-1.27}=5.37\times 10^{-2}
\]

\[
K_{a2}=10^{-4.28}=5.25\times 10^{-5}
\]

For a diprotic acid, the fraction present as \(\ce{C2O4^{2-}}\) is

\[
\alpha_2=\frac{K_{a1}K_{a2}}{[\ce{H+}]^2+K_{a1}[\ce{H+}]+K_{a1}K_{a2}}
\]

Since

\[
[\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]=\alpha_2 C_T
\]

\[
\alpha_2=\frac{2.7\times 10^{-8}}{0.100}
=2.7\times 10^{-7}
\]

So

\[
2.7\times 10^{-7}
=
\frac{(5.37\times 10^{-2})(5.25\times 10^{-5})}
{[\ce{H+}]^2+(5.37\times 10^{-2})[\ce{H+}]+(5.37\times 10^{-2})(5.25\times 10^{-5})}
\]

\[
K_{a1}K_{a2}=2.82\times 10^{-6}
\]

Because \(\alpha_2\) is very small, the denominator is approximately

\[
\frac{2.82\times 10^{-6}}{2.7\times 10^{-7}}
=10.44
\]

Thus

\[
[\ce{H+}]^2+0.0537[\ce{H+}]+2.82\times 10^{-6}\approx 10.44
\]

\[
[\ce{H+}]\approx 3.21\ \text{M}
\]

\[
\text{pH}=-\log(3.21)
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{pH}\approx -0.51}
\]

---

e. Final solution contains \(0.100\ \text{mol}\) calcium and \(0.100\ \text{mol}\) total oxalate. The amount of chloride added must balance charge.

At pH \(\approx -0.51\),

\[
[\ce{H+}]\approx 3.21\ \text{M}
\]

In 1.00 L,

\[
n(\ce{H+})\approx 3.21\ \text{mol}
\]

The solution also contains

\[
0.100\ \text{mol}\ \ce{Ca^{2+}}
\]

giving \(0.200\) mol positive charge from calcium.

Almost all oxalate is present as neutral \(\ce{H2C2O4}\), with only small amounts of \(\ce{HC2O4^-}\) and \(\ce{C2O4^{2-}}\). Thus the chloride needed is approximately

\[
n(\ce{Cl^-})\approx n(\ce{H+})+2n(\ce{Ca^{2+}})
\]

\[
n(\ce{HCl})\approx 3.21+0.200=3.41\ \text{mol}
\]

A slightly more exact correction for the small amount of \(\ce{HC2O4^-}\) is negligible.

\[
\boxed{3.41\ \text{mol HCl}}
\]

---

f. In \(0.100\ \text{M}\ \ce{NaHC2O4}\), there is already a large concentration of oxalate-containing species. The relevant equilibrium is

\[
\ce{HC2O4^- <=> H+ + C2O4^{2-}}
\]

with

\[
K_{a2}=5.25\times 10^{-5}
\]

For an amphiprotic ion \(\ce{HC2O4^-}\),

\[
\text{pH}\approx \frac{1}{2}(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})
\]

\[
\text{pH}\approx \frac{1}{2}(1.27+4.28)=2.78
\]

\[
[\ce{H+}]\approx 10^{-2.78}=1.7\times 10^{-3}\ \text{M}
\]

Then

\[
\frac{[\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]}{[\ce{HC2O4^-}]}
=\frac{K_{a2}}{[\ce{H+}]}
=\frac{5.25\times 10^{-5}}{1.7\times 10^{-3}}
\approx 0.031
\]

So

\[
[\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]\approx 0.031(0.100)=3.1\times 10^{-3}\ \text{M}
\]

This is much larger than the oxalate concentration in pure water from dissolution of calcium oxalate, about \(5.2\times 10^{-5}\ \text{M}\).

Therefore, by the common-ion effect, the solubility is approximately

\[
s=\frac{K_{sp}}{[\ce{C2O4^{2-}}]}
=\frac{2.7\times 10^{-9}}{3.1\times 10^{-3}}
\approx 9\times 10^{-7}\ \text{M}
\]

This is far smaller than

\[
5.2\times 10^{-5}\ \text{M}
\]

so the solubility is significantly less than in pure water.

\[
\boxed{\text{Significantly less than in pure water, due to the common-ion effect from oxalate.}}
\]

turns.question:
N,N-Dimethylethanolamine ((CH3)2NCH2CH2OH, DMEA, M = 89.14) is a Brønsted base whose conjugate acid, DMEAH+, has a pKa = 9.22 (Ka = 6.0 x 10-10). Acetic acid (CH3COOH, M = 60.05) has a pKa = 4.75 (Ka = 1.8 x 10-5).
a. Calculate ∆G°rxn at 298 K for the acid-base reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH.
A solution consisting of 7.84 g CH3COOH and 107.17 g water is placed in a well-insulated (Dewar) flask. To this solution is added DMEA in small portions. After each portion of DMEA is added, the solution is stirred and the temperature measured with a digital thermometer. The data obtained are plotted, showing a linear relationship y = 1.141x + 19.03 for < 12 g added DMEA, and a plateau at an average of y = 31.84 for >= 12 g added DMEA (where y is temperature in °C and x is mass of DMEA in g).
b. Calculate ∆H°rxn for the reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH. You may assume that all solutions have the same specific heat capacity as pure water.
c. Calculate ∆S°rxn for the reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH.
d. The ∆S° calculated in part c. is negative. What features of the reaction of DMEA with CH3COOH cause it to have a negative entropy of reaction?
turns.official_answer:
a. -25.5 kJ mol-1
b. -51.6 kJ mol-1
c. -87.6 J mol-1 K-1
d. The reaction produces two charged particles from two neutral ones, leading to stronger solvation and decreased entropy.

Part b: 4 points (1 pt for finding intersection mass, 1 pt for qrxn, 1 pt for moles reacted, 1 pt for ∆H°rxn).
Part c: 3 points (2 pts for setup, 1 pt for ∆S°).
Part d: 2 points (2 pts for explaining solvation of charged particles).

turns.candidate_answer:
We consider the acid-base reaction

\[
\ce{DMEA + CH3COOH -> DMEAH+ + CH3COO^-}
\]

---

### a. Calculate \(\Delta G^\circ_{\rm rxn}\) at 298 K

For a proton-transfer reaction,

\[
\ce{B + HA -> BH+ + A^-}
\]

the equilibrium constant is related to the acid dissociation constants by

\[
K=\frac{K_a(\ce{HA})}{K_a(\ce{BH+})}
\]

Here,

\[
K=\frac{K_a(\ce{CH3COOH})}{K_a(\ce{DMEAH+})}
=\frac{1.8\times 10^{-5}}{6.0\times 10^{-10}}
\]

\[
K=3.0\times 10^4
\]

Then

\[
\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K
\]

\[
\Delta G^\circ=-(8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(298\ \text{K})\ln(3.0\times 10^4)
\]

\[
\ln(3.0\times 10^4)=10.31
\]

\[
\Delta G^\circ=-2.55\times 10^4\ \text{J/mol}
\]

\[
\boxed{\Delta G^\circ_{\rm rxn}\approx -25.5\ \text{kJ/mol}}
\]

---

### b. Calculate \(\Delta H^\circ_{\rm rxn}\)

Initial solution contains acetic acid and water:

\[
m_{\ce{CH3COOH}}=7.84\ \text{g}
\]

\[
n_{\ce{CH3COOH}}=\frac{7.84\ \text{g}}{60.05\ \text{g/mol}}
=0.1306\ \text{mol}
\]

The temperature rises linearly with added DMEA until all acetic acid has reacted, then reaches a plateau.

The equivalence mass of DMEA is

\[
m_{\rm eq}=n_{\ce{CH3COOH}}M_{\rm DMEA}
\]

\[
m_{\rm eq}=(0.1306\ \text{mol})(89.14\ \text{g/mol})
=11.64\ \text{g}
\]

From the initial linear fit,

\[
T=1.141x+19.03
\]

At \(x=11.64\ \text{g}\),

\[
T_f=1.141(11.64)+19.03
\]

\[
T_f=32.31^\circ\text{C}
\]

Initial temperature from the fit is

\[
T_i=19.03^\circ\text{C}
\]

Thus

\[
\Delta T=32.31-19.03=13.28^\circ\text{C}
\]

Assume the solution has the same heat capacity as water. The total mass of solution at equivalence is

\[
m_{\rm soln}=107.17+7.84+11.64=126.65\ \text{g}
\]

Heat absorbed by the solution:

\[
q_{\rm soln}=m_{\rm soln}c\Delta T
\]

\[
q_{\rm soln}=(126.65\ \text{g})(4.184\ \text{J g}^{-1}\!^\circ\text{C}^{-1})(13.28^\circ\text{C})
\]

\[
q_{\rm soln}=7.04\times 10^3\ \text{J}
\]

The reaction released this heat, so

\[
q_{\rm rxn}=-7.04\times 10^3\ \text{J}
\]

Per mole of reaction:

\[
\Delta H^\circ_{\rm rxn}
=\frac{-7.04\times 10^3\ \text{J}}{0.1306\ \text{mol}}
\]

\[
\Delta H^\circ_{\rm rxn}=-5.39\times 10^4\ \text{J/mol}
\]

\[
\boxed{\Delta H^\circ_{\rm rxn}\approx -53.9\ \text{kJ/mol}}
\]

Using the observed plateau \(31.84^\circ\text{C}\) instead of the extrapolated equivalence temperature gives a very similar value, about \(-52\ \text{kJ/mol}\).

---

### c. Calculate \(\Delta S^\circ_{\rm rxn}\)

Use

\[
\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ
\]

so

\[
\Delta S^\circ=\frac{\Delta H^\circ-\Delta G^\circ}{T}
\]

\[
\Delta S^\circ
=\frac{-53.9\ \text{kJ/mol}-(-25.5\ \text{kJ/mol})}{298\ \text{K}}
\]

\[
\Delta S^\circ
=\frac{-28.4\ \text{kJ/mol}}{298\ \text{K}}
\]

\[
\Delta S^\circ=-0.0953\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}
\]

\[
\boxed{\Delta S^\circ_{\rm rxn}\approx -95\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}}
\]

---

### d. Why is \(\Delta S^\circ\) negative?

The reaction converts two neutral molecules into two oppositely charged ions:

\[
\ce{DMEA + CH3COOH -> DMEAH+ + CH3COO^-}
\]

Charged ions in water strongly organize surrounding water molecules into hydration shells. This ordering of solvent molecules decreases entropy.

Also, the product ions experience electrostatic interactions and are more constrained in solution than the neutral reactants. Therefore, even though the number of solute particles is roughly unchanged, solvent ordering around the newly formed ions dominates.

\[
\boxed{\text{The negative entropy is mainly due to formation of ions, which causes strong ordering of surrounding water molecules.}}
\]

Part c correctly applies the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation. Part d correctly attributes negative entropy to solvent ordering by charged ions.
judge_result.deductions: In part b, the candidate calculated the equivalence mass from stoichiometry instead of finding the intersection of the two experimental temperature lines, which affected the enthalpy and subsequent entropy values.

turns.question:
A galvanic cell is set up with a Zn electrode in 1.00 M Zn2+(aq) and a Pb electrode in 1.00 M Pb2+(aq), connected by a salt bridge. The cell potential measured as a function of temperature gives a linear graph with the equation E = 0.7887 - 0.000515 T (where E is in V and T is in K).
a. Which electrode is the anode and which is the cathode?
b. The standard reduction potential for Zn2+(aq) at 298 K is –0.762 V. What is the standard reduction potential for Pb2+(aq) at 298 K?
c. What are ∆G° (at 298 K), ∆H°, and ∆S° for the reaction shown below?

\[
\ce{O}: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4
\]

The three \(2p\) orbitals are degenerate. By Hund’s rule, electrons occupy separate degenerate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing. Thus the \(2p^4\) configuration has two unpaired electrons:

\[
2p:\ \uparrow\downarrow\quad \uparrow\quad \uparrow
\]

So atomic oxygen has two unpaired electrons.

For molecular oxygen, the molecular orbital configuration for the valence electrons is

\[
(\sigma_{2s})^2(\sigma^*_{2s})^2(\sigma_{2p})^2(\pi_{2p})^4(\pi^*_{2p})^2
\]

The two highest-energy electrons occupy two degenerate antibonding \(\pi^*\) orbitals. By Hund’s rule, they occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, so \(\ce{O2}\) also has two unpaired electrons.

\[
\boxed{\text{Both have two unpaired electrons because degenerate orbitals are singly occupied before pairing.}}

\[
\boxed{\ce{O2}\text{ is IR-inactive because its vibration does not change dipole moment; }\ce{O3}\text{ is IR-active because its vibrations do.}}

- \(\ce{O2+}\): remove one electron from antibonding \(\pi^*\), bond order \(=2.5\), shortest.
- \(\ce{O2}\): bond order \(=2\).
- \(\ce{O2^-}\): add one electron to antibonding \(\pi^*\), bond order \(=1.5\).
- \(\ce{O2^{2-}}\): add two electrons to antibonding \(\pi^*\), bond order \(=1\), longest.

\[
\ce{O2+} < \ce{O2} < \ce{O2^-} < \ce{O2^{2-}}

\boxed{\text{type D small spheres}=\ce{O}}
\]

This is also consistent with the described coordination environments of the black spheres, since copper in \(\ce{YBa2Cu3O7}\) occurs in square-planar and square-pyramidal oxygen coordination environments.

---

### e. Oxidation numbers in \(\ce{YBa2Cu3O7}\)

Oxygen is normally

\[
\ce{O}=-2
\]

so seven oxygens contribute

\[
7(-2)=-14
\]

Yttrium is normally

\[
\ce{Y}=+3
\]

Barium is an alkaline earth metal:

\[
\ce{Ba}=+2
\]

Two barium atoms contribute

\[
2(+2)=+4
\]

Let the average oxidation number of copper be \(x\). Charge balance:

\[
(+3)+2(+2)+3x+7(-2)=0
\]

\[
3+4+3x-14=0
\]

\[
3x=7
\]

\[
x=+\frac73
\]

Thus the average copper oxidation state is

\[
\boxed{\ce{Cu}=+\frac73\text{ on average}}
\]

This corresponds formally to a mixture of copper oxidation states, commonly written as one \(\ce{Cu^{3+}}\) and two \(\ce{Cu^{2+}}\) per formula unit:

\[
2(+2)+1(+3)=+7
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\ce{Y}=+3,\quad \ce{Ba}=+2,\quad \ce{O}=-2,\quad \ce{Cu}=+\frac73\text{ average}}
\]

or

\[
\boxed{\text{formally }2\ce{Cu^{2+}}\text{ and }1\ce{Cu^{3+}}\text{ per formula unit}}
\]

---

### f. Coordination geometries of the black spheres and relation to oxidation numbers

The black spheres are copper atoms.

The description says:

- The top and bottom face copper sites each have four nearest oxygen neighbors arranged at the corners of an approximately flat square.
- The middle-layer copper sites have those four near-coplanar oxygen neighbors plus one additional nearest oxygen neighbor along the vertical axis.

Therefore, the two copper coordination geometries are:

\[
\boxed{\text{square planar } \ce{CuO4}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\text{square pyramidal } \ce{CuO5}}
\]

This relates to the oxidation states because the three copper atoms are not all equivalent. The average copper oxidation state is \(+\frac73\), which implies mixed-valence copper, usually described as a combination of \(\ce{Cu^{2+}}\) and \(\ce{Cu^{3+}}\). Different copper sites have different oxygen coordination environments, so they can have different electron densities/formal oxidation-state character.

\[
\boxed{\text{The distinct Cu geometries reflect crystallographically different Cu sites and are consistent with mixed-valence Cu.}}
\]

Many organic compounds react with elemental halogens such as Br2 or I2.
a. Under appropriate conditions, 3-methylpentane will react with Br2 to form a single monobromide with the formula C6H13Br. Give appropriate reaction conditions and the structural formula of the product.
b. Cyclohexene forms different products when reacted with Br2 in water than when reacted in carbon tetrachloride. Give structural formulas for the products formed in the two solvents, including stereochemistry if relevant.
c. Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst. Give an example of a suitable catalyst and the structural formula of the major organic product of the reaction.
d. Cyclopentanone reacts with excess bromine in the presence of base to give a tetrabromide. Give a structural formula for the product and explain why the reaction does not give good yields of a monobromide product even when only one equivalent of Br2 is used.
e. Acetophenone, C6H5COCH3, reacts with excess iodine in the presence of aqueous sodium hydroxide to give a yellow precipitate and a water-soluble organic species. Give structural formulas for these two products.
turns.official_answer:
a. Conditions: Free radical conditions (photolysis or benzoyl peroxide). Product: 3-bromo-3-methylpentane.
b. In water: trans-2-bromocyclohexan-1-ol. In CCl4: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
c. Catalyst: AlBr3 or FeBr3. Product: bromobenzene.
d. Product: 2,2,5,5-tetrabromocyclopentan-1-one. The monobromoketone is more acidic than cyclopentanone, leading to polybromination.
e. Products: CHI3 (iodoform) and sodium benzoate (C6H5COONa).

### a. Radical bromination of 3-methylpentane

To obtain a single major monobromide, use radical bromination conditions:

\[
\boxed{\ce{Br2,\ h\nu}}
\]

or heat/light.

3-Methylpentane has one tertiary hydrogen at carbon 3. Bromination is highly selective for the tertiary C–H bond, so the product is 3-bromo-3-methylpentane:

\[
\boxed{\ce{CH3CH2C(Br)(CH3)CH2CH3}}
\]

Reaction:

\[
\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3 + Br2 ->[h\nu] CH3CH2C(Br)(CH3)CH2CH3 + HBr}
\]

---

### b. Reaction of cyclohexene with \(\ce{Br2}\)

#### In carbon tetrachloride

In non-nucleophilic solvent such as \(\ce{CCl4}\), bromine adds across the double bond through a bromonium ion, giving anti addition.

Product:

\[
\boxed{\text{trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane}}
\]

Structural description: bromines are on adjacent carbons, one wedge and one dash.

\[
\boxed{\ce{trans-C6H10Br2}}
\]

It is formed as a racemic mixture of enantiomers.

#### In water

In water, the bromonium ion is opened by water, giving a bromohydrin. Addition is anti, with \(\ce{OH}\) and \(\ce{Br}\) trans to each other. For cyclohexene, the two alkene carbons are equivalent, so only one constitutional product forms.

Product:

\[
\boxed{\text{trans-2-bromocyclohexanol}}
\]

or equivalently trans-1-bromo-2-hydroxycyclohexane.

Structural description: adjacent \(\ce{Br}\) and \(\ce{OH}\), one wedge and one dash.

\[
\boxed{\ce{trans-C6H10(Br)(OH)}}
\]

Also formed as a racemic mixture.

---

### c. Bromination of benzene

Benzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with bromine in the presence of a Lewis acid such as

\[
\boxed{\ce{FeBr3}}
\]

or \(\ce{AlBr3}\).

Major product:

\[
\boxed{\ce{C6H5Br}}
\]

bromobenzene.

\[
\ce{C6H6 + Br2 ->[FeBr3] C6H5Br + HBr}
\]

---

### d. Bromination of cyclopentanone in base

Cyclopentanone has four \(\alpha\)-hydrogens total, two on each carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. In base, ketones form enolates, and \(\alpha\)-bromination occurs. Because the product remains acidic at the \(\alpha\)-positions and bromine substituents increase acidity, repeated bromination occurs readily.

With excess bromine, all four \(\alpha\)-hydrogens are replaced.

Product:

\[
\boxed{\text{2,2,5,5-tetrabromocyclopentanone}}
\]

Structural description: cyclopentanone ring with the carbonyl carbon as C1, and two bromines on each adjacent carbon C2 and C5:

\[
\boxed{\ce{O=C1-C(Br)2-CH2-CH2-C(Br)2-1}}
\]

The reaction does not give good yields of monobromide even with one equivalent of \(\ce{Br2}\) because base-catalyzed halogenation is autocatalytic toward further substitution: each bromine substituent makes remaining \(\alpha\)-hydrogens more acidic, so the monobromoketone forms enolate more readily than the starting ketone and is brominated faster.

\[
\boxed{\text{Further bromination is faster than initial bromination, so mixtures/polybrominated products result.}}
\]

---

### e. Iodoform reaction of acetophenone

Acetophenone is a methyl ketone:

\[
\ce{C6H5COCH3}
\]

With excess iodine in aqueous base, it undergoes the haloform reaction.

The yellow precipitate is iodoform:

\[
\boxed{\ce{CHI3}}
\]

The remaining water-soluble organic species is the carboxylate salt, sodium benzoate:

\[
\boxed{\ce{C6H5COO^- Na^+}}
\]

or structurally:

\[
\boxed{\ce{C6H5-C(=O)O^-}}
\]

as its sodium salt.

Overall organic products:

\[
\boxed{\ce{CHI3\ (yellow\ precipitate) + C6H5COO^-}}
\]
